# ON FLUIDITY

<meta>continues from previous page: oil of sweet almonds, instead of common oil.</meta>

...we distinguished from the two most recent examples mentioned, because in those cases we assume that some of the external <term>corpuscles</term> <gloss>tiny particles of matter</gloss> remain within that body, contributing to its firmness and (though perhaps only in a very small amount) entering into its constitution; whereas in this case we assume that they do not materially combine to form the body upon which they act, but merely agitate and variously move the particles composing it. They do this perhaps by breaking some, bending and entangling others, and, in a word, changing the <term>texture</term> <gloss>structural arrangement</gloss> so that those parts which were previously either moving separately or were less tightly bound together are now reduced into a narrower space or a more intricate structure, and in this way are more firmly connected to each other.

That the bare arrangement of the parts of a body, by which they regard one another, can contribute greatly to stability without the addition of any external matter, may be seen both in certain examples mentioned before and in willow twigs <note>original Latin: "virgis vimineis"</note>. When these lie loose in a pile, each can easily be separated from the rest; but when they are woven into a basket <note>original Latin: "quasillum"</note>, they cling together so firmly that if one is lifted, all the rest are raised with it. <summary>Boyle argues that the firmness of a substance can result from a mechanical change in the arrangement and entanglement of its existing particles rather than the addition of new material. He illustrates this through the analogy of loose twigs becoming a sturdy structure when woven into a basket.</summary>
